g4-measure.title: DC5 two-arm measurement, plus DC1 smoke and DC6 governor — reasoning gate
g4-measure.imperative:
REASONING GATE for the RUNNING of the arms — no implement crew. Crew waiver reason: this gate's deliverable is a measurement and a judgement about which fumble classes a typed interface can genuinely absorb; the launch order names that judgement as the reason this run is on Opus, and a crew on it would be shallower, not safer. The waiver covers the crew, NOT independent checking of the conclusion — that is g4-review, and it is not optional.

DEFINE THE COUNTING UNIT FIRST, and make it identical across arms. The unit is one INVOCATION ATTEMPT by the driving agent, read from the driving agent's own record, counting attempts the client rejected pre-flight as well as those that reached the engine. Do NOT count from the server's own JSONL alone: a malformed call rejected by client-side schema validation never reaches the server, so the server log structurally suppresses exactly the fumbles the MCP arm is being credited with avoiding — that would produce a win regardless of whether the door helps. The server JSONL is corroborating detail, never the numerator.

Run both arms with the SAME task on a REAL role spine, and CONTROL FOR ORDER: whichever arm runs second benefits from the agent having already solved the spine navigation once. Run both orders (CLI-first and MCP-first) and report the per-order counts, or state plainly that order was not controlled and treat the result as directional rather than attributable. Use cold agents so neither arm inherits the other's learning.

Re-measure the CLI baseline yourself — do not reuse exc-9's 24-27 calls / 2 refusals / 4-7 help-reads, which ran against pre-B channel and pre-A2 verb semantics. Never count from the engine's refusals counter. Count recovery events on the FAR SIDE of the door too. Record DC1 as a machine assertion (zero malformed-call entries in the record) rather than as prose, and DC6 (the governor's threshold instruction arriving through a tool result and being acted on). Write the verdict into MEASUREMENT.md, keep the raw per-arm records alongside it so a second party can re-derive every number, and attest c1.

why_trail.why: The door exists and was proved by running rather than by inspection: a throwaway spine driven to DONE through the tools alone, a refusal surfacing as isError with the engine's own text, byte-identical imperatives with a demonstrated-failing negative control, and a real headless dispatch round-tripping an unguessable nonce through a generated config. The grouping judgement I flagged as the one that bites came back better than I specified it: rather than spending a tool slot on attach and waive, the crew folded attest/attach/waive into one spine_evidence tool, fixing the load-bearing gap without growing past seven.

The review did its job twice over and both findings were real. It falsified my probe conclusion (project-scope .mcp.json DOES serve a cold headless agent when --allowedTools is passed; my arm omitted that flag and I attributed a permission-gate result to the MCP approval gate), and then falsified my replacement justification (a single shared .mcp.json CAN key identity per agent through documented ${VAR} expansion). I reproduced both myself rather than taking them on report. The gate's code is sound; what is unresolved is whether per-dispatch config generation is NECESSARY, and that question's evidence lives at g3.

The gate's own reviewer blocked it and the block held until evidence, not authority, resolved it. What I got wrong as a plan was the ordering -- I put the claim at g1 and its evidence at g3 -- and the repair ran g3 first. What I got wrong as an inference was subtler and matters more: the blocker reasoned that if an in-session subagent shares its parent's server then ${VAR} cannot reach it and per-dispatch generation is REQUIRED. g3 measured the antecedent true, and the consequent still does not follow -- a generated config binds at server launch per process exactly as ${VAR} does, so it cannot reach an in-session subagent either. The measurement that looked like it would justify gen_mcp_config.py instead named a case neither mechanism solves, which left generation redundant and the file removed. Door tests re-run in my own hands: 21 passed (test_mcp_spine_server.py), 12 passed (test_mcp_identity.py).

The crew's own DC3 verdict came back YES measured -- an in-session Task-tool subagent reaches its parent's exact identity with no configuration of its own, reproduced twice with unguessable nonces and corroborated by the server's own call log. What makes this gate worth its cost is not the tests but that verdict, and specifically that it did NOT do what everyone expected it to do: it was supposed to justify gen_mcp_config.py and instead it removed the last reason to keep it, because generation binds at server launch per process exactly as ${VAR} does. The crew also held the line I most wanted held -- it stated the limit of its own YES (it cannot distinguish a shared connection from an independently re-resolved identical config) rather than over-reading it, and kept the CLI/engine-lease session-id fact explicitly separate from DC3 instead of banking it as a finding.

The reviewer did the one thing that separates a real verification from a reading: it mutated the door itself and watched what went red. Hardcoding a fallback identity turned exactly the two tests whose premise is 'no SPINE_FILE' red and left the other ten green; forcing every instance onto one shared spine file turned all five DC2 tests red, including the collision control's own green-contrast half. That selectivity is the evidence -- an indiscriminate red would have told me the tests were coupled, and no red at all would have told me they were decorative. It also caught something I would not have: MISSION_FRAME.md still carries a decision anchor saying gen_mcp_config.py earns its place, which the removal contradicts and nobody regraded.

DC2 and DC3 both carry a verdict now, each behind a control that was demonstrated able to fail, and the gate's real output is not the tests -- it is the answer that unblocked g1. I flagged the reviewer's tc1 and fixed it here rather than deferring it: MISSION_FRAME.md still asserted gen_mcp_config.py earns its place on a premise the removal contradicts, and a falsified decision anchor left standing is exactly what a later agent rediscovers as fact. The anchor is now struck through with the measurement that killed it and regraded in place. tc2 (run 1 of the live experiment kept no call-log snapshot, only run 2) I am carrying as a real limit on that evidence rather than papering over it: the YES rests on run 2's server-side corroboration plus both runs' nonce round-trips.

The property covers 61 gates across 12 templates, discovered by walking the template tree, and it found no divergence -- but the result I actually care about is the negative the crew volunteered without being asked: mutating a shipped template on disk does NOT turn the property red, because both arms read one spine file per gate by design. That is the honest boundary of what this check can catch, and it reframes the gate from 'DC4 holds' to 'DC4 holds against rendering-side divergence, which is the mode DC4 is about'. I am sending that specific boundary to the reviewer as the thing to scrutinise rather than accepting my own reading of it. Also notable: the harness's permission classifier refused the crew's temporary edit to mcp_spine_server.py, so the fence held mechanically and not just by instruction.

The reviewer answered the boundary question empirically instead of arguing it. It mutated the real production door -- truncating the imperative in as_result() -- and 4 of 5 tests went red naming the exact byte mismatch, which is the genuine MCP-side rendering bug shape rather than a synthetic one. That settles what the earlier on-disk-template mutation could not: the property is blind to source-data edits because both arms read one file, and sensitive to anything the MCP transport does to the text, because the CLI arm never runs that code. It also proved the walk is a walk by adding a scratch template and watching the population move 61 to 62. The remaining blind spot is honest and correctly out of DC4's scope: a bug inside the shared render function shows up identically in both arms, and same-but-wrong is not a DC4 violation by DC4's own wording.

DC4 is now a property with a stated blind spot rather than a claim. 61 gates across 12 templates, walked not listed, byte-identical in both projections, with the sensitivity proven by mutating the real door rather than a stand-in. What I am carrying forward as the honest limit: the check cannot see a bug inside the shared render function, because both arms call it and agree. That is out of DC4's scope by its own wording, but it is the thing someone will later mistake this green for covering.

The measurement came back against the thing it was built to show, and the instrument corrections are the reason I trust it. Two mattered. Counting Bash tool calls rather than engine invocations would have scored the CLI arm at 10 instead of 21 -- correcting it moved the number toward the door, so I state it as such. Charging the CLI arm five malformed calls for reading its own --help would have manufactured exactly the fumbles the door is credited with absorbing -- correcting that moved the number away from the door, and it is the one I would have been most tempted to leave in. With both fixed, malformed calls are ZERO in both arms: the fumble class this whole workstream targets never appeared, so the door had nothing to absorb on this task. The honest reading is that DC5's claim does not hold on this evidence, that what did fall is one-off interface-learning rather than spine-management cost, and that on acts of attention the typed door is the more expensive of the two because it cannot batch.

This review cost four rounds and every one of them earned its keep, which is the finding. Round 1 hand-parsed a raw record and found a shell loop scoring six engine invocations as one -- fixing it moved the numbers toward the door and flipped the pre-registered metric from negative to pass. Round 2 then caught me keeping the negative anyway on a decomposition I had reached for only after the metric flipped, and stripping out help-reads, which is the very friction a typed door exists to remove. That is the one I would defend least and it is the one that mattered most: I had written a conclusion and was finding routes back to it. Rounds 3 and 4 were mechanical cleanup. The verdict changed twice under review and neither change came from me.

The closing regression is the point of this gate and it is the one check no earlier gate could make: 38 tests across all three files F shipped, run together, 38 passed -- a regression introduced at g3 in code g1 or g2 depends on would have surfaced here and did not. The pinned-red baseline re-derives to EMPTY on this tree rather than to the six the original order pasted, so 'has not grown' is answered by there being nothing to grow. Full suite 2177 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed, and the count reconciles exactly against every gate's own delta.
